standard.title: Language to express preferences
standard.description: explore different ways of using language to express preferences, likes and dislikes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students bring natural oral language for expressing feelings. They have not yet been asked to consciously identify or compare the specific language choices used to express preferences, or to recognise how these are conveyed in visual and media texts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify and use a range of language choices for expressing preferences, likes and dislikes — in speech, gesture and visual forms — and can compare how different choices work.

nodes.label: Preferences can be put into words
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express a like, dislike or preference using words, and recognise that language is one way to communicate feelings.
nodes.minimum_width: Express one like or dislike using a word or phrase (e.g. 'I love...', 'I don't like...').
nodes.typical_width: Express preferences, likes and dislikes in words; explore different word choices for the same feeling (e.g. 'like', 'love', 'enjoy', 'prefer').
wider: Collect and compare words for positive and negative preferences from classroom picture books
Explore vocabulary for feelings and preferences in languages other than English known to students in the class

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of preference language beyond the immediate 'like/don't like' binary. A vocabulary repertoire is what this node is building.

success_criteria: Student uses at least one specific word or phrase to express a preference beyond 'like' or 'don't like'.
Student can identify that language was used to express a feeling or preference.

nodes.label: Gesture and speech work together
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise that feelings and preferences are communicated through both language and body — speech and gesture work together.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate one gesture (e.g. thumbs up, facial expression) that communicates a preference, and pair it with a spoken word.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise how feelings and preferences are communicated in speech and gesture; practise combining gesture and language to express preferences more fully.
wider: Compare how preferences are expressed through gesture in different cultural contexts — noticing that gestures are not universal
Explore how animated characters (in animations or picture books) use body language and speech together to communicate feelings

response_modes.reason: Students may initially treat gesture as decoration — the misconception is that words alone carry meaning. Multiple contexts showing gesture as a meaning-making system help resolve this.

success_criteria: Student can describe how both words and gesture are used to show how a character or person feels.
Student can demonstrate expressing a preference using both spoken language and an appropriate gesture.

nodes.label: Preferences in visual and media texts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how emotions and preferences are conveyed in visual and media texts — not just through words but through images, colour, and sound.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how one visual text (e.g. an advertisement or animation) shows a character or person feeling a preference.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise how emotions and feelings are conveyed in visual and media texts such as advertising and animations; identify specific visual and multimodal choices that communicate preference.
wider: Compare how two different advertisements or animations convey emotions and preferences — what visual choices do they make?
Explore how texts by First Nations Australian creators use visual language to convey feelings and preferences
Investigate how colour and facial expression in picture book illustrations signal character preferences without words

response_modes.reason: The concept (preferences communicated through multiple modes) requires multiple text types before it generalises — advertising and animation are explicitly named in elaborations, and each medium uses different conventions.
Here students bring together language, gesture and visual knowledge — connecting all three as modes for expressing preferences. The coordination across modes is the learning.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The multimodal dimension — how visual texts signal preferences — is genuinely rich at Foundation. Students can explore advertising, animation, illustration and digital media, with real opportunity for media literacy development beyond what's strictly necessary.
success_criteria: Student can identify at least one visual or sound feature in a media text that communicates a feeling or preference.
Student can explain how that feature communicates the feeling — not just say that it does.
